clue.text: Justified being collected

blocks.note: first meaning: warranted, the opposite of uncalled for
second meaning: fetched, as a parcel or a child waiting to be picked up

explanation.walkthrough: Read as one phrase it sounds like a claim about someone who stays calm; the two halves are separate senses of the same phrase, CALLED FOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Something warranted is needed by the situation, and a person waiting to be fetched is one somebody will come round for.

clue.text: Caught fish with stick

blocks.note: c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
the ling is a long sea fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: An angler lands a fish using a rod.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' looks like the rod the fish was caught with; it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To cling is to hold fast or adhere, the verb sense of stick.

clue.text: Auction sale-room sending one to sleep

definitions.text: Auction sale-room sending one to sleep

blocks.note: setter's reading: at an auction, bidders signal by nodding, so the room is a realm of nodding
surface reading: a dull sale that makes one drowse; the realm of sleep in the phrase

explanation.walkthrough: The Land of Nod is the proverbial place of sleep, from Genesis via a pun on nodding off; at an auction a nod is a bid.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names sleep as a country, and an auction room is literally where people nod.

clue.text: Get mixed up between Lords and Wimbledon in London

definitions.note: the answer is a district in London

blocks.note: earls are lords, peers of the realm
Wimbledon's tennis is played on grass courts

explanation.surface: Someone confuses Lord's cricket ground with the Wimbledon tennis venue.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is London's famous cricket ground and Wimbledon its tennis championship; read instead as peers and a playing surface. The opening words are not fully accounted for.
explanation.definitionFit: Earls Court is a district of west London, known for its exhibition centre.

clue.text: Servant who might walk out

definitions.note: a person who travels on foot, read as two words

blocks.note: first meaning: a liveried household attendant
second meaning, split in two: a man on foot, a pedestrian

explanation.surface: A domestic employee who could go on strike at any moment.
explanation.walkthrough: Walking out suggests quitting; read the answer as foot plus man and it is someone who goes about walking.
explanation.definitionFit: A liveried attendant in a great house, who historically ran beside his employer's carriage on foot.

clue.text: Sailor comes back with little particles of food

indicators.note: coming back is returning the way one came, so the seaman's word runs from its end

blocks.note: a tar is a sailor
ions are charged atoms or molecules, tiny particles

explanation.surface: A seaman returns bringing crumbs of something to eat.
explanation.definitionFit: Rations are fixed allowances of provisions, so the word stands for food supplies.

clue.text: Sweet stuff puts Surrey right on top

blocks.note: Sy is the old postal abbreviation for the county of Surrey
R is the usual abbreviation for right
on top means up, above

explanation.surface: A boast that some confection lifts the county of Surrey to first place.
explanation.walkthrough: Surrey is a county just south of London; its abbreviation Sy is the uncommon convention here.
explanation.definitionFit: Syrup is a thick sugary liquid, so it is literally a sweet substance.

clue.text: In this way the Financial Times goes to tender

blocks.note: so means thus, in this way
FT is the newspaper's own abbreviation

explanation.surface: The newspaper thus submits a bid for a contract.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tender' looks like a business bid; it is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft and tender both describe something yielding, gentle to the touch or easily bruised.

clue.text: Animal makes money

blocks.note: first meaning: the horned African or Asian beast
second meaning: old British slang for cash

explanation.surface: Some creature earns a living.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhinoceros is shortened to rhino, and rhino has been dated slang for cash since the 1600s.

clue.text: Commandeer the services of a lot of reporters

blocks.note: first meaning: to force someone into doing a job
second meaning: a group of journalists, the press as a gang

explanation.surface: An editor seizes a crowd of journalists for a story.
explanation.definitionFit: Press-ganging was forced naval recruitment, now any coercion into service; read literally it is a band from the press.

clue.text: Someone called to the bar near miss

blocks.note: first meaning: a member of the ... Temple, one of the Inns of Court where barristers qualify
second meaning: on a target, the ring next to the bull is a shot that just fails

explanation.surface: A barrister narrowly fails to be admitted to the legal profession.
explanation.walkthrough: Being called to the bar is qualifying as a barrister in England; the Inner Temple is one of the four Inns that do it.
explanation.definitionFit: In archery and darts the ring nearest the bullseye is called the inner, a shot that only just misses the centre.

clue.text: Deprived of railway unlike everybody else

blocks.note: to be out of something is to be without it
a railway line, or simply a line

explanation.surface: Someone cut off from the train service feels singled out from everyone around them.
explanation.definitionFit: To be out of line is to step away from what others do, behaving differently from the group.

clue.text: Complaint over Othello being shot in August

definitions.note: the place where the shooting happens, not the thing shot

blocks.note: to grouse is to complain, and a grouse is a complaint
Shakespeare's Othello is the Moor of Venice

explanation.surface: A grievance about Othello being gunned down one summer month.
explanation.walkthrough: Grouse shooting in Britain opens on 12 August, and is done on heather moorland; the definition describes the place by what happens there.
explanation.definitionFit: Open upland heath where red grouse are bred and driven towards guns once the season starts in mid-August.

clue.text: What must be done for a kick-off

definitions.text: What must be done for a kick-off

blocks.clueFragment: What must be done for a kick-off
blocks.note: surface reading: a requirement before a game can start, or before anything begins
setter's reading: before a football match the captains flip a coin to choose ends and who kicks off

explanation.walkthrough: It sounds like a general riddle about getting started; the answer is the coin flip that settles which side starts a football match.
explanation.definitionFit: Spinning a coin is the routine way referees decide who begins play at the start of a match.

clue.text: People near sewage works are likely to be unpopular

blocks.note: first meaning, taken literally: surrounded by a nasty smell
second meaning: the idiom for being out of favour

explanation.surface: Residents living beside a treatment plant tend to be disliked.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is meant literally, a whiff from the works; the second is the everyday idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in bad odour is an idiom for being in disfavour, and it literally describes an unpleasant smell.

clue.text: Scotsman quickly gets wind

blocks.note: mon is the Scots form of man
soon means before long, quickly

explanation.surface: A Scot who eats too fast ends up with indigestion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind' tempts you to read flatulence after a hurried meal; it is a weather wind.
explanation.definitionFit: A monsoon is the seasonal wind of South Asia that brings heavy rains.

clue.text: Grumbled at mum subordinate to editor

blocks.note: ma is mother
a subordinate is under someone
ed is the standard abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: A junior journalist complained about his mother, who works beneath the editor.
explanation.walkthrough: Maunder is now usually to ramble, but its older sense is to mutter complaints.
explanation.definitionFit: To maunder is to talk in a dreary, muttering, complaining way.

clue.text: Artisan trained as a singer

indicators.note: training reshapes something, so the letters of the craftsman's word are put into new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A craftsman who has had lessons to become a vocalist.
explanation.definitionFit: Frank Sinatra was the celebrated American crooner, so his surname is an example of a vocalist.

clue.text: Fortunate occasion for quality broadcast

blocks.note: first meaning: as in the saying '... lucky'
second meaning: airtime on the BBC Third Programme, its highbrow radio channel

explanation.surface: A lucky moment to put out a high-class programme.
explanation.walkthrough: The BBC Third Programme, from 1946 to 1970, broadcast serious music and talk; the second half reads as time on the Third.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb 'third time lucky' makes the third attempt the one that succeeds.

clue.text: Travel by tube for experience

blocks.note: the tube is London's underground railway, so travelling by it takes you below ground
to go is to travel

explanation.surface: Riding the London Underground as a way of seeing life.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tube is the everyday name for the London Underground; the pieces come out in reverse clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: To undergo something is to experience it, to go through it.

clue.text: Work you allowed to be borrowed is very rich

blocks.note: op is short for opus, a work
U is the text-speak form of you
lent means handed over on loan

explanation.surface: A wealthy person's piece of work that he let you borrow.
explanation.definitionFit: Opulent means luxuriously wealthy, displaying great riches.

clue.text: Station of the cross?

blocks.note: surface reading: one of the Stations of the Cross, the devotional scenes of Christ's road to crucifixion
setter's reading: a railway station whose name the word cross completes

explanation.walkthrough: The Christian Stations of the Cross are the false path; the answer is the first word of a London railway terminus, Charing Cross.
explanation.definitionFit: Charing Cross is a main London railway terminus, so this word is the part of that station's name that goes before Cross.

clue.text: Her colt can utter a gleeful sound

indicators.note: what a horse can utter is noise in a muddle, loosely signalling that the letters come out reordered

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A mare's foal is able to make a happy noise.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal is loose; the surface almost works as a whole, a young horse laughing.
explanation.definitionFit: A chortle is a gleeful, snorting chuckle, a word coined by Lewis Carroll.

clue.text: Land is cut off

blocks.note: first meaning: to bring a ship in to berth, or a spacecraft to join another
second meaning: to shorten

explanation.surface: A territory has been isolated from its neighbours.
explanation.definitionFit: Docking a vessel brings it to shore, and docking a tail or wages removes part of it.

clue.text: Bird with its head covered

blocks.note: first meaning: a castrated cockerel fattened for the table
second meaning, read as two words: having a hat on

explanation.surface: A fowl wearing something on its head.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer into CAP ON and it describes a hat being worn.
explanation.definitionFit: A capon is a castrated domestic cock raised for eating, so it is a kind of bird.

clue.text: Former monk is not allowed ...

definitions.note: the answer means not allowed; is is part of the phrase it replaces

blocks.note: first meaning: someone who has left a religious order
second meaning: against the rules

explanation.surface: An ex-monk is forbidden from passing himself off as one these days.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots carry the sentence on into 25 across, which has its own answer; this clue's two meanings sit before them.
explanation.definitionFit: A monk who has left belongs to no religious order any more, and conduct against the rules is said to be improper in a meeting.

clue.text: Swindles requiring the right amount of current

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right
amps measure electric current

explanation.surface: Frauds that need just the correct electrical supply.
explanation.walkthrough: A ramp is British slang for a swindle, especially an inflated price.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a ramp is a racket or fraudulent scheme, so ramps are cons.

clue.text: Papers about in the morning

blocks.note: re means concerning, about
a.m. marks morning hours

explanation.surface: Newspapers arriving at some point before noon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Papers' suggests newspapers; it means sheets.
explanation.definitionFit: A ream is a standard quantity of sheets, 480 or 500, sold as a bundle.

clue.text: ... to pass off about now

definitions.note: an infinitive; the answer is the bare verb

blocks.note: re means about, concerning
the present is now

explanation.surface: Continuing 22: a former monk may not pass himself off as one these days.
explanation.definitionFit: To represent something as genuine is to pass it off as such, presenting it falsely.

clue.text: Only a dope would confuse PM with IOU

indicators.note: mixing two things up muddles their letters together into a jumble

blocks.note: taken as written
joins the two sets of letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: Only an idiot could mix up a prime minister with a promissory note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dope' reads as a fool; it is the drug.
explanation.definitionFit: Dope is slang for a narcotic, and opium is the classic narcotic drug made from poppies.

clue.text: Material is dug up the wrong way

indicators.note: going the wrong way means running back to front, so the word is read from its end

blocks.note: mined means dug up from the ground

explanation.surface: Fabric that has been excavated by mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: Denim is a hard-wearing cotton cloth, the fabric jeans are made of.

clue.text: Horrible sensation could make a pest cheer

indicators.note: making something out of material means building it into a new form, so the letters are rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A nuisance cheering you up would feel ghastly.
explanation.definitionFit: The creeps is a feeling of fear or revulsion, an unpleasant shiver.
